What would be the best way to implement tilemaplayer chucnking?
Should we have tiles in their own layers, or create a new tilemap every ~1,000,000 tiles or something?

> Changing the quadrant size to anything other than 16 crashes the game with: Element limit reached
(I tried setting it to 2/4/8/32/64)

Yeah, there's a hard limit on the amount of canvas items RIDs the engine can use, and I guess you reached it. Or maybe you are out of memory, I am not sure. So well, in any case there's no way around that.

> What would be the best way to implement tilemaplayer chucnking?

I think a single tilemap, with dynamically added/removed chunks depending on the camera position should work. For that you can use the TileMapPattern class, it is basically a data container that allows you to paste its content into a TileMapLayer node. You can also use https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_tilemaplayer.html#class-tilemaplayer-method-get-pattern to get a pattern from set of coordinates. I'd suggest taking a chunk size similar to the quadrant size, or multiplied with 2 or 3 (like, 32x32 or something).

You could also use different TileMapLayers, but that means duplicating the node and working around the API a bit.  It's done that way there: https://github.com/Voidbrew/chunk_manager

> I tried messing with the TileMapPattern and didn't notice any improvement.. unless i'm missing something here..

I mean, the point is to dynamically load / unload chunks. You should have a only a few chunks loaded at the same time. TileMapPattern is just for convenience, and can also help if you need to generate things in a thread for example.

> Even when using get_pattern and set_pattern i still have lag when deleting a tile.. I don't understand why there isn't a more efficient way to modify tiles without the tilemaplayer needing to go over every tile again. Especially considering only a small percent of my world is being rendered in my viewport.. am i just missing something?

You need to erase/add tiles again in your TileMapLayer depending on the chunks you need. Rendering is only part of what's loaded, and, while the cells exists whether it is visible or not, there are still many things that are kept in the memory. 

>  yet i am able to delete tiles in real time with no performance hit at all. But when i try the same thing with the TIleMapLayer, it freezes up every time a tile is deleted.. Is that because the entire TileMapLayer is being redrawn or scanned over each time a tile is deleted? I don't see why it would need to go over the entire TileMapLayer if only a small percent of the TileMap is being rendered in my viewport.. Sorry if i am asking dumb questions or entirely misunderstand whats going on.

TileMapLayers internam updates should be individual or chunked depending on the system (physics, rendering, custom data, etc.) so modifying a single tile shouldn't hurt theoretically. However, some debug features/modifying the TileSet can trigger full updates. 

> Here is the script i made to attempt to use the TileMapPattern. Is this method the correct usage?

No, that's not the usage I had in mind. You need to start with an empty TileMapLayer and fills it in dynamically according to the player's position. The problem is having millions of cells set in your TileMapLayer, not really the method you use to update them.

> No, that's not the usage I had in mind. You need to start with an empty TileMapLayer and fills it in dynamically according to the player's position. The problem is having millions of cells set in your TileMapLayer, not really the method you use to update them.

Well there's no way around that for me.. as i'm making a Terraria style game. The world is generated with millions of tiles before the player ever enters the scene.... Then if i were to start creating multiple TileMapLayers for individual chunks i feel like it would over complicate everything..  
I already disabled physics, collisions, navigation and everything imaginable thinking it would help with performance but it didn't.. i mean the game runs flawlessly until trying to delete a single tile...  And i feel like it would be a lot of work to implement breaking the tilemap into separated nodes / chunks, especially with synchronizing it all in multiplayer instances.. 

Again i just feel like deleting a single tile shouldnt be this complicated... or maybe im just dumb

> Well there's no way around that for me.. as i'm making a Terraria style game. The world is generated with millions of tiles before the player ever enters the scene.... Then if i were to start creating multiple TileMapLayers for individual chunks i feel like it would over complicate everything..

I mean. I am quite sure terraria does not keep the whole world in memory while you are exploring it. Or maybe it does, but keeps nothing related to rendering loaded at all. You should either dynamically load tiles from disk, or, like, use a custom data structure (an array/matrix) to keep things even more simple. Then the strategy could be to dynamically update a TileMapLayer according to what's inside the data structure and needs to be loaded/rendered.

Internally, TileMaps are using a HashMap, which can end up a bit slow with huge worlds, but is memory efficient in sparse worlds. Once you reach a given amount of tiles, yes, coming up with your own custom-designed solution is better anyway.
TileMapLayer is optimized for middle-sized worlds, but anything beyond that will require custom data structures and dynamic loading.

> Again i just feel like deleting a single tile shouldnt be this complicated... or maybe im just dumb

Deleting a single tile is not complicated, it's deleting a tile in a data structure of millions of entries that can end up complicated. Since per-subsystem data is chunked, updating a tile in a chunk updates the whole chunk, which can usually be more costly than expected. I don't deny there might be some inefficiencies here and there, but you have to be reasonable about the performances you can expect from multi-purpose game engine. We sadly have to find a balance between features-completeness and performances.

So well, games like factorio/terraria/noita aren't really use case covered by the default TileMapLayer implementation I'd say.

Hmm. TileMap-specific updates are done in batch at the end of a frame (via `call_deferred`). And I believe nothing runs on the physics tick there. I don't know what could cause the lag spike in physics tick.

@TheLoneInitiate I'm like 99% Terraria, and other games like it, chunk the world. I know someone made a realistic scale game set in Great Britain, in Godot, and pulled it off thanks to implementing chunking. Check out the Godot subreddit, they described at least parts of how they did the chunking

There is simply NO way for ANY engine to work with millions of tiles around

@Zireael07 Well i do generate the world in chunks, but didnt store the data and access it in chunks.. and well considering i made my own custom tilemap system yesterday that is generating even larger worlds than i was generating with the tilemap nodes and it has no performance issues tells me that the current tilemap system in godot could use some improvements.. 

And the main question here is : Why is the Physics Time in the profiler spiking by 300+ms when deleting a tile, even when all the physics functionality in the tilemap node have been disabled entirely.... it seems like something is off.

> and it has no performance issues tells me that the current tilemap system in godot could use some improvements.

As I already mentioned, TileMap has a tons of features to fit many different use cases. It is completely expected that a custom, tailor-made solution performs better than a general purpose one.

> And the main question here is : Why is the Physics Time in the profiler spiking by 300+ms when deleting a tile, even when all the physics functionality in the tilemap node have been disabled entirely.... it seems like something is off.

Physics tick does not mean it's a process related to physics. It can be completely unrelated. Physics ticks are just ran at a consistent rates (like, 60 times per second), while frames tick can be executed a lot more often (depending on the game performance). In general, physics is indeed ran in the physics tick, but a lot of processing completely unrelated to physics is ran also in the physics step. So you are assuming wrong in thinking the problem here is related to physics. The problem can be from any other thing.

> Edit: I can't even load the MRP on my side, it hangs for minutes.

I had a similar problem on an unoptimized build. I had to compile with `optimize=speed_trace` to get it to be performant enough to open, which then took about 10s.

I worked on Starbound and can confirm it's all chunked. Even then 8400x2400 is about as large as the largest world size we had, that's quite a large size to process without using a specialty system. It's actually not that large of an amount of data from the perspective of just loading it locally, but without chunking I'd expect the performance to be pretty bad for anything past that unless you're using something very specialized.

That said, I figured I would look at this as a stress test and see if there were any obvious bottlenecks, and there were two that jumped out on the flamegraph.

The first is that, while navigation is disabled, any update will cause every cell to clear their navigation regions. Clearing the regions only if navigation was just disabled removes all of the visible stutter in the MRP for me.

The second was a bunch of overhead from the red black tree used to sort quadrants. I tried out `LocalVector` and `SortArray` instead to see how it would compare, and it's uglier but significantly faster.

#### Numbers
With navigation disabled, I get ~260 ms Physics spikes.
With navigation enabled, I get ~40 ms Physics spikes. If you need a temporary workaround, you may actually get better performance by enabling navigation.
With navigation disabled and the first optimization, I get ~40 ms Physics spikes.
With navigation disabled and both optimizations, I get < 30 ms Physics spikes.

At that point, the process time (~50 ms) dominates. Further improvements would be more complicated, since the time is then dominated by a mix of sorting and calculating cull information.

> Potentially resolved with [#109243](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/109243)

It's a partial resolution, debatably a full one but I wasn't willing to unilaterally state that since it still takes more than a frame's worth of CPU time. It still feels like there's improvements that can be made, I just handled the low hanging fruit, but it does vastly improve the situation and I don't think there are further easy wins.

If others think this level of improvement constitutes a full fix, neat, works for me.
